subject: Mathematics
title: Arun's Friendship Rules
hook: Can friendship be a function? Arun discovers relations and functions through his boarding school friend groups.

characters.name: Coach Vikram
characters.role: Sports coach, explains domain and range

slides.title: Relations and Functions
slides.storyContext: Arun arrives at boarding school and notices patterns in how students connect.

slides.title: The Friendship Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arun's dorm has 4 students: Arun (A), Priya (P), Rohan (R), and Zara (Z). Arun notices: A is friends with P and R; P is friends with A and Z; R is friends with A; Z is friends with P. He asks Coach Vikram if this friendship pattern follows a rule.

slides.title: What is a Relation?
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram explains: A relation is ANY set of ordered pairs. Friendship from person X to person Y is (X, Y).

points.label: Definition
points.text: A relation R from set A to set B is a subset of A × B (the Cartesian product).

points.label: Example in the story
points.text: Friendship relation = {(A,P), (A,R), (P,A), (P,Z), (R,A), (Z,P)}. Not every pair is friends — (A,Z) is NOT in the relation.

slides.inSimpleWords: A relation is a connection or pairing between things. It doesn't have to follow a strict rule — any subset of pairs works.

slides.title: Arun Maps the Friendships
slides.storyContext: Arun draws arrows: A→P, A→R, P→A, P→Z, R→A, Z→P. He realizes this is just a visual way to show the relation — every arrow is one ordered pair.

slides.title: Cartesian Product Explained
slides.storyContext: Priya introduces the Cartesian product: if A = {A, P} and B = {R, Z}, then A × B contains all possible pairs (first from A, second from B).

points.label: Definition
points.text: A × B = {(x, y) : x ∈ A, y ∈ B}. Every element of A paired with every element of B.

points.label: Size
points.text: If |A| = m and |B| = n, then |A × B| = m × n.

points.label: Example
points.text: {A, P} × {R, Z} = {(A,R), (A,Z), (P,R), (P,Z)}. Four ordered pairs total.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cartesian product is all possible pairings. A relation picks SOME of these pairs, not necessarily all.

slides.title: Finding Relations from Cartesian Product
slides.storyContext: Arun practices identifying relations. Given A = {1, 2} and B = {a, b}, list A × B and then identify specific relations.

points.label: Example relation 1
points.text: R₁ = {(1,a), (2,b)} (a 2-pair relation)

points.label: Example relation 2
points.text: R₂ = {(1,a), (1,b), (2,a)} (a 3-pair relation)

example.problem: List all possible relations from {1,2} to {a,b}. How many are there?
example.solution: A × B has 4 elements. A relation is any subset of these 4 pairs. Number of subsets = 2⁴ = 16. They range from the empty relation ∅ to the complete relation {(1,a), (1,b), (2,a), (2,b)}.

slides.inSimpleWords: A relation is a chosen subset of the Cartesian product. You can have 0, some, or all pairs.

slides.title: Domain and Range
slides.storyContext: Coach asks: Who are all the students doing the friending (the 'from' side)? Who are all the students being friended (the 'to' side)?

points.label: Domain
points.text: The set of all first elements (inputs): {A, P, R, Z}. Who are the ones doing the action?

points.label: Range
points.text: The set of all second elements (outputs): {A, P, R, Z}. Who are the ones receiving the action?

example.problem: For the relation R = {(A,P), (A,R), (P,A), (P,Z), (R,A), (Z,P)}, find domain and range.
example.solution: Domain = {A, P, R, Z}. Range = {P, R, A, Z} = {A, P, R, Z}.

slides.inSimpleWords: Domain = who sends the relation. Range = who receives it.

slides.title: Finding Domain and Range from Pairs
slides.storyContext: Priya gives Arun practice: look at relation S = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1), (2,4)}. What are the domain and range?

points.label: Step 1: List all first elements
points.text: Domain = {1, 2, 3}

example.problem: For S = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1), (2,4)}, identify domain and range.
example.solution: Domain: all unique first coordinates = {1, 2, 3}. Range: all unique second coordinates = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Note: 4 is in range but not domain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scan the ordered pairs. First coordinates form the domain; second coordinates form the range.

slides.title: Arun's Realization about Relations
slides.storyContext: Arun realizes friendships are symmetric sometimes (if A is friends with P, often P is friends with A) but not always required. Relations don't need any symmetry or consistency — they're just flexible pairings.

slides.title: Properties of Relations
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram teaches Arun about four key properties relations can have.

points.label: Reflexive
points.text: Every element is related to itself: (x,x) ∈ R for all x. Example: 'equals' is reflexive because 5 = 5.

points.label: Symmetric
points.text: If (x,y) ∈ R, then (y,x) ∈ R. Example: 'is the same age as' is symmetric.

points.label: Transitive
points.text: If (x,y) ∈ R and (y,z) ∈ R, then (x,z) ∈ R. Example: 'is an ancestor of' is transitive.

points.label: Equivalence
points.text: If a relation is reflexive, symmetric, AND transitive, it's an equivalence relation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Relations can have patterns: self-loops (reflexive), reversals (symmetric), and chains (transitive). Some have all three (equivalence).

slides.title: Identifying Relation Properties
slides.storyContext: Priya quizzes Arun on whether relations have these properties.

points.label: Friendship relation
points.text: Usually not reflexive (people don't list themselves as friends). Often symmetric. May not be transitive (friends of friends ≠ friends).

points.label: 'Is divisible by'
points.text: Reflexive (6 divides 6). Not symmetric (2 divides 6, but 6 doesn't divide 2). Transitive (if 6 divides 12 and 12 divides 24, then 6 divides 24).

points.label: 'Is equal to'
points.text: Reflexive, symmetric, AND transitive. This is an equivalence relation.

example.problem: Is the relation 'is the same height as' reflexive, symmetric, and transitive?
example.solution: Yes to all. Reflexive: you're the same height as yourself. Symmetric: if you're the same height as a friend, they're the same height as you. Transitive: if you and friend 1 are the same height, and friend 1 and friend 2 are the same height, then you and friend 2 are the same height. This is an equivalence relation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check if (x,x) is in R (reflexive), if reversals work (symmetric), and if chains work (transitive).

slides.title: What is a Function?
slides.storyContext: Arun realizes: in the classroom, EVERY student has EXACTLY ONE class teacher. This is different from friendship — some have no friends, some have many, but EVERY student has ONE teacher. Priya calls this a function.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A function f: A → B is a special relation where every element of A maps to EXACTLY ONE element of B. No element is left out; no element maps to two different values.

points.label: Vertical Line Test
points.text: If a relation is shown as a graph, a vertical line crosses it at most once ⟹ it's a function.

example.problem: Is f = {(A,P), (A,R), (P,Z), (R,A), (Z,P)} a function from {A,P,R,Z} to itself?
example.solution: No. A maps to both P and R (two outputs). In a function, A must map to exactly one value.

slides.inSimpleWords: A function is a relation with a strict rule: each input has ONE and ONLY ONE output.

slides.title: The Class Teacher Example
slides.storyContext: In the class roster, each student (A, P, R, Z) is assigned exactly one class teacher. Arun→Ms. Sharma, Priya→Mr. Singh, Rohan→Ms. Sharma, Zara→Mr. Singh. This is a function: every student has one teacher, though two students can share the same teacher.

slides.title: Testing Whether a Relation is a Function
slides.storyContext: Priya gives Arun several relations to check. For each, ask: does every input have exactly one output?

points.label: R₁ = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,4)}
points.text: Yes, this is a function. Each input (1, 2, 3) has one output.

points.label: R₂ = {(1,2), (1,3), (2,4)}
points.text: No. Input 1 maps to both 2 and 3. Not a function.

points.label: R₃ = {(1,5), (2,5), (3,5)}
points.text: Yes, this is a function. All inputs map to the same output (5). That's allowed.

example.solution: Yes. Each input (2, 3, 4, 5) appears exactly once, mapping to a unique output (1, 2, 3, 4 respectively).

slides.inSimpleWords: Function check: does each input appear at most once? If yes, it's a function. If any input appears twice with different outputs, it's not.

slides.title: Types of Functions
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram introduces three important types through school scenarios.

points.label: One-to-one (Injective)
points.text: Different students get different class teachers. No two students share the same teacher.

points.label: Onto (Surjective)
points.text: Every teacher in the school teaches at least one student. No teacher is left without a class.

points.label: Bijective (One-to-one AND Onto)
points.text: Perfect pairing: each student has one unique teacher, and each teacher has one unique student. This is reversible (has an inverse).

slides.inSimpleWords: Injective = no collisions (different inputs → different outputs). Surjective = all outputs are used. Bijective = perfect match both ways.

slides.title: Classifying Functions: Injective, Surjective, Bijective
slides.storyContext: Priya quizzes Arun on three scenarios involving student-to-teacher mappings.

points.label: Scenario 1: Injective?
points.text: f = {(A, Ms.S), (P, Mr.Si), (R, Ms.S), (Z, Mr.Si)}. No: both A and R map to Ms.S (not injective).

points.label: Scenario 2: Surjective?
points.text: f = {(A, Ms.S), (P, Mr.Si), (R, Ms.S), (Z, Mr.Si)}. Yes, if the codomain is {Ms.S, Mr.Si} — every teacher is assigned.

points.label: Scenario 3: Bijective?
points.text: f = {(A, Ms.S), (P, Mr.Si), (R, Ms.T), (Z, Mr.N)}, codomain = {Ms.S, Mr.Si, Ms.T, Mr.N}. Yes: each student gets one unique teacher, and each teacher gets one unique student.

example.problem: Is the function mapping {1,2,3}→{a,b,c} defined by f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=c bijective?
example.solution: Yes. Different inputs → different outputs (injective), and every element of {a,b,c} is mapped to (surjective). So it's bijective.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check if every input is unique (injective), every output is used (surjective), or both (bijective).

slides.title: Inverse Function
slides.storyContext: If teacher Ms. Sharma teaches Arun (f: Arun → Ms. Sharma), then the inverse asks: which student does Ms. Sharma teach? (f⁻¹: Ms. Sharma → Arun). Only bijective functions have inverses.

points.label: Inverse exists only for bijective functions
points.text: f⁻¹ exists ⟺ f is both injective and surjective.

points.label: Property
points.text: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x and f⁻¹(f(x)) = x for all x in the domain.

example.problem: If f(x) = 2x + 3, find f⁻¹(x).

slides.inSimpleWords: The inverse function reverses the direction: if f takes input to output, f⁻¹ takes the output back to the original input.

slides.title: Challenge: Find the Inverse
slides.storyContext: Arun works through finding inverses. Given f(x) = 3x − 5, can he find f⁻¹(x)?

example.problem: Find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 3x − 5, then verify.

slides.inSimpleWords: Swap x and y, solve for the new y, then verify both directions compose to x.

slides.title: Composition of Functions
slides.storyContext: Arun realizes: first, the class teacher assigns students to projects (f). Then, the project groups go to different labs (g). The combined route (student → project group → lab) is the composition g∘f.

points.label: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x))
points.text: Apply f first, then g to the result. Order matters: g∘f ≠ f∘g usually.

example.problem: If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, find (g∘f)(3) and (f∘g)(3).
example.solution: (g∘f)(3) = g(f(3)) = g(4) = 8. (f∘g)(3) = f(g(3)) = f(6) = 7. Different answers — order matters!

slides.inSimpleWords: Composition chains functions: do f first, then g. Like getting dressed: socks (f), then shoes (g). Can't do it backwards the same way.

slides.title: Composition in Practice
slides.storyContext: At a science fair, Arun sees this flow: student ID (f)→ assigned lab, lab (g)→ equipment checklist. So (g∘f)(student ID) = equipment checklist. Composing functions tracks complex workflows.

slides.title: Computing Compositions Step-by-Step
slides.storyContext: Priya walks Arun through a composition problem where two functions are combined.

points.label: Let f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 5
points.text: Find (f∘g)(3) and write the formula for (f∘g)(x).

points.label: Step 2: Apply f to the result

example.problem: Write the formula for (f∘g)(x) where f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Substitute the inner function g(x) into f. Simplify to get the combined formula.

slides.title: Challenge: Verify Bijective and Find Inverse
slides.storyContext: Priya gives Arun a puzzle: The dorm assigns each student a unique room number. f(x) = 2x − 1 maps x ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4} to room numbers. Is this a bijection from {1, 2, 3, 4} to {1, 3, 5, 7}? If yes, find the inverse.

example.problem: Show that f(x) = 2x − 1 is bijective on the given sets and find f⁻¹.
example.solution: f(1) = 1, f(2) = 3, f(3) = 5, f(4) = 7. All outputs are distinct (injective) and all outputs {1,3,5,7} are covered (surjective). So bijective. Inverse: f⁻¹(y) = (y + 1)/2. Verify: f⁻¹(1) = 1, f⁻¹(3) = 2, f⁻¹(5) = 3, f⁻¹(7) = 4. ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Bijective means perfect one-to-one pairing with all outputs used. If so, you can always reverse it.

slides.title: Properties of Functions
slides.storyContext: Priya summarizes properties that Arun should know when working with functions.

points.label: Identity function
points.text: f(x) = x. Every element maps to itself. Always bijective.

points.label: Constant function
points.text: f(x) = c (same output for every input). Surjective only if codomain = {c}; never injective if domain has >1 element.

points.label: Commutative property (addition/multiplication)
points.text: f(x) + g(x) = g(x) + f(x). Addition and multiplication of function outputs are commutative.

slides.inSimpleWords: Identity = x→x. Constant = x→5 (always). Functions inherit properties from their operations.

slides.title: Practical: Who Can and Cannot Have Inverses?
slides.storyContext: Arun checks which functions are invertible. Not all can be reversed.

points.label: f(x) = x² (domain = ℝ)
points.text: Not bijective: f(2) = f(−2) = 4 (not injective). Can't find a unique inverse.

points.label: f(x) = x² (domain = [0,∞))
points.text: Bijective if codomain = [0,∞). Injective (no duplicates in [0,∞)) and surjective (all non-negatives covered). Inverse: f⁻¹(x) = √x.

points.label: f(x) = 2^x
points.text: Injective (different x → different outputs), surjective if codomain = (0,∞). Bijective. Inverse: f⁻¹(x) = log₂(x).

example.problem: Explain why f(x) = x² is not invertible on ℝ but is invertible on [0,∞).
example.solution: On ℝ: both 2 and −2 map to 4, violating injectivity. On [0,∞): each non-negative output comes from exactly one non-negative input, so it's bijective and invertible.

slides.inSimpleWords: Restricting the domain can turn a non-invertible function into an invertible one.

slides.title: Challenge: Composition and Inverses
slides.storyContext: Priya poses a harder puzzle: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = 3x, find (g∘f)⁻¹(x). Does (g∘f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹?

example.problem: Find (g∘f)⁻¹ and verify (g∘f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.

slides.inSimpleWords: The inverse of a composition reverses the order: (g∘f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹. Like undressing: shoes off first, then socks.

slides.title: Arun's Realization
slides.storyContext: By mid-semester, Arun sees that friendships are just relations (flexible, multiple friends possible), while assigned roles (class teacher, dorm room) are functions (strict, one-to-one). Understanding this helps him think about data and patterns everywhere.

slides.title: What Arun Learned
slides.storyContext: Arun now understands how friendships differ from assigned class roles.

points.text: A relation is ANY set of ordered pairs; a function is a relation where each input has exactly one output.
Domain = set of all inputs; Range = set of all outputs.
Injective (one-to-one) = different inputs give different outputs. Surjective (onto) = all outputs are used.
Bijective = both injective and surjective; only bijective functions have inverses.
Composition g∘f means: apply f first, then g. Order matters. Inverse of composition reverses order: (g∘f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.

slides.inSimpleWords: Relations are flexible pairings. Functions are strict: one input → one output. Some functions can be reversed (bijections); most cannot.

subject: Mathematics
title: Kavya's Angle Hunt
hook: Kavya's drone footage reveals angles hidden in nature. She learns to find angles using inverse trig functions.

slides.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
slides.storyContext: Kavya's drone captures a temple tower casting a shadow. She knows the height and shadow length — but needs to find the angle of elevation. Arjun introduces inverse trig functions.

slides.title: The Temple Tower Mystery
slides.storyContext: Kavya's drone spots Meenakshi Temple. The tower is 50 meters tall and casts a 50-meter shadow on flat ground. What is the angle of elevation from the shadow tip to the tower top? If sin(θ) = y, then arcsin(y) gives θ back. That's the inverse.

slides.title: What are Inverse Trig Functions?
slides.storyContext: Arjun explains: Trig functions take an angle and give a ratio (e.g., sin(30°) = 0.5). Inverse trig functions take a ratio and give back an angle.

points.label: arcsin (or sin⁻¹)
points.text: If sin(θ) = y, then arcsin(y) = θ. Returns angles in [−π/2, π/2].

points.label: arccos (or cos⁻¹)
points.text: If cos(θ) = y, then arccos(y) = θ. Returns angles in [0, π].

points.label: arctan (or tan⁻¹)
points.text: If tan(θ) = y, then arctan(y) = θ. Returns angles in (−π/2, π/2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Inverse trig functions reverse the direction: instead of angle → ratio, they do ratio → angle.

slides.title: Kavya's First Angle
slides.storyContext: From the drone footage: tower height 50m, shadow 50m. Tangent of the angle = opposite/adjacent = 50/50 = 1. Arjun asks: which angle has tangent = 1? Kavya realizes she needs arctan(1) = 45°.

slides.title: Why Inverse Trig Functions Need Restricted Domains
slides.storyContext: Arjun explains: sine, cosine, and tangent are not one-to-one over their full domains. To make inverses, we restrict them.

points.label: The problem
points.text: sin(30°) = 0.5, but also sin(150°) = 0.5. Two angles give the same sine!

points.label: The solution
points.text: Restrict sine domain to [−π/2, π/2] so it's bijective. Then arcsin is well-defined.

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: Without restrictions, there would be infinite answers to 'find the angle where sin(θ) = 0.5.'

slides.inSimpleWords: Trig functions repeat their outputs. To invert them, we limit the domain so each ratio has exactly one angle.

slides.title: Domain and Range of Inverse Functions
slides.storyContext: Nisha teaches Kavya: each inverse trig function has a specific range (where it outputs angles). This ensures it's a true function (one-to-one).

points.label: arcsin: domain [−1, 1], range [−π/2, π/2]
points.text: For any y between −1 and 1, arcsin(y) gives an angle between −90° and 90°.

points.label: arccos: domain [−1, 1], range [0, π]
points.text: For any y between −1 and 1, arccos(y) gives an angle between 0° and 180°.

points.label: arctan: domain (−∞, ∞), range (−π/2, π/2)
points.text: For any real number y, arctan(y) gives an angle between −90° and 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each inverse has limits: sine/cosine/tangent values must be in a specific range for the inverse to work.

slides.title: Basic Inverse Trig Values
slides.storyContext: Arjun teaches Kavya common arcsin, arccos, arctan values she'll see often.

points.label: arcsin(0.5) = π/6 = 30°
points.text: Because sin(30°) = 0.5.

points.label: arccos(0.5) = π/3 = 60°
points.text: Because cos(60°) = 0.5.

points.label: arctan(1) = π/4 = 45°
points.text: Because tan(45°) = 1.

example.problem: Find arcsin(√3/2) and arctan(√3).

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorize the standard ratios: sin/cos/tan of 30°, 45°, 60°, then their inverses follow immediately.

slides.title: Kavya Builds Her Angle Toolkit
slides.storyContext: Kavya writes down a reference table: sin(0°) = 0, sin(30°) = 0.5, sin(45°) ≈ 0.707, sin(60°) ≈ 0.866, sin(90°) = 1. Now she can quickly reverse them using arcsin.

slides.title: The Temple Tower Problem Solved
slides.storyContext: Kavya applies arctan: tower height = 50 m, shadow = 50 m. So tan(θ) = 50/50 = 1. What angle has tan = 1?

points.label: Setup
points.text: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent = height/shadow = 50/50 = 1.

points.label: Apply arctan
points.text: θ = arctan(1) = π/4 radians = 45°.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The angle of elevation from shadow tip to tower top is 45°.

example.problem: A ladder leans against a wall. The ladder is 10 m long, and its base is 6 m from the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

slides.inSimpleWords: Know the ratio (sine, cosine, or tangent value), use the inverse function to find the angle.

slides.title: Challenge: Finding Angles from Ratios
slides.storyContext: Arjun gives Kavya more angle-finding puzzles from drone measurements.

example.problem: From drone footage: opposite side = 35 m, hypotenuse = 50 m. What is the angle of elevation?

slides.inSimpleWords: Identify the ratio (sin, cos, or tan) from the triangle, then apply the inverse to get the angle.

slides.title: Common Angles and Their Inverse Values
slides.storyContext: Kavya memorizes key inverse values to speed up her calculations.

points.label: arcsin(0) = 0, arcsin(1) = π/2, arcsin(−1) = −π/2
points.text: Extreme values of sine.

points.label: arccos(0) = π/2, arccos(1) = 0, arccos(−1) = π
points.text: Extreme values of cosine.

points.label: arctan(0) = 0, arctan(∞) → π/2, arctan(−∞) → −π/2
points.text: Behavior of arctan at extremes.

example.problem: Evaluate arccos(1) and arcsin(−1).

slides.inSimpleWords: Boundary and special values help you check answers and work faster.

slides.title: Inverse Cotangent, Secant, Cosecant
slides.storyContext: Nisha mentions three more inverse functions, less common but important for full coverage.

points.label: arccot: domain (−∞, ∞), range (0, π)
points.text: If cot(θ) = y, then arccot(y) = θ.

points.label: arcsec: domain (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞), range [0, π] \ {π/2}
points.text: If sec(θ) = y, then arcsec(y) = θ.

points.label: arccsc: domain (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞), range [−π/2, π/2] \ {0}
points.text: If csc(θ) = y, then arccsc(y) = θ.

slides.inSimpleWords: These are less common but follow the same idea: ratio → angle, with specific ranges to ensure one-to-one mapping.

image.alt: Inverse Cotangent, Secant, Cosecant — Inverse Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Angle of Depression from Elevation
slides.storyContext: Nisha explains: angle of depression (looking down) is equal to angle of elevation (looking up) by alternate interior angles. Kavya's drone often measures both.

points.label: Same magnitude
points.text: If you look down at 30°, and someone at ground level looks up at you, they see a 30° angle of elevation.

points.label: Triangle property
points.text: In a right triangle, if one angle is θ, the other non-right angle is 90° − θ.

example.problem: From a 20 m high drone, Kavya looks down at an object 15 m away horizontally. Find the angle of depression.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angle of depression and angle of elevation are equal by geometry. They're mirror angles on a slanted line.

slides.title: Key Identities
slides.storyContext: Arjun lists formulas Kavya will use often when solving problems involving inverse trig.

points.label: arcsin(x) + arccos(x) = π/2
points.text: For any x ∈ [−1, 1].

points.label: arctan(x) + arccot(x) = π/2
points.text: For any x ∈ ℝ.

points.label: sin(arcsin(x)) = x
points.text: For x ∈ [−1, 1]. The function and its inverse cancel.

slides.inSimpleWords: These identities let you rewrite and simplify equations involving inverse trig functions.

slides.title: Using the Identity arcsin(x) + arccos(x) = π/2
slides.storyContext: Arjun shows Kavya how to use this identity to verify or simplify calculations.

points.label: If arcsin(0.6) ≈ 0.6435 radians
points.text: Then arccos(0.6) = π/2 − 0.6435 ≈ 0.9273 radians (about 53.13°).

example.problem: If arccos(0.8) = θ, find arcsin(0.8) in terms of θ or numerically.
example.solution: Using the identity: arcsin(0.8) + arccos(0.8) = π/2. So arcsin(0.8) = π/2 − arccos(0.8) = π/2 − θ ≈ 1.5708 − 0.6435 ≈ 0.9273.

slides.inSimpleWords: The identity links arcsin and arccos. If you know one, you can quickly find the other.

slides.title: Bridge Construction Problem
slides.storyContext: Nisha's company plans a foot-bridge over a river. From point A on one bank, the angle of elevation to the top of a pole on the opposite bank is 30°. The horizontal distance is 20 m. Find the pole height.

points.label: Given
points.text: Angle of elevation θ = 30°, horizontal distance = 20 m.

points.label: Setup
points.text: tan(30°) = height / 20.

example.problem: Find the pole height.
example.solution: tan(30°) = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577. Height = 20 × tan(30°) = 20 / √3 = 20√3 / 3 ≈ 11.55 m. Alternatively: if height = h, then 30° = arctan(h/20), so h = 20 · tan(arctan(h/20)). Direct: h = 20 · tan(30°) ≈ 11.55 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you know an angle and one side, trig gets you the other. When you know sides and need the angle, inverse trig is your tool.

image.alt: Bridge Construction Problem — Inverse Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Kavya at the Construction Site
slides.storyContext: Nisha takes Kavya to a real bridge project. Surveyors use inverse trig constantly: measuring angles with theodolites, calculating heights and distances. Kavya's drone does the same thing, just from the air.

slides.title: Two-Point Distance and Angle Calculation
slides.storyContext: Kavya needs to find the distance between two points using only angle and altitude measurements.

points.label: From drone at height h = 100 m
points.text: Looking at point P with angle of depression 25°. Find horizontal distance to P.

points.label: Formula
points.text: tan(angle of depression) = height / horizontal distance.

example.problem: Drone at 50 m height sees target at angle of depression 18°. How far away?

slides.inSimpleWords: From altitude and angle, find distance using tan(angle) = height / distance.

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-Angle Problem
slides.storyContext: Kavya's drone measures angles from two locations. From point P, the angle of elevation to a cloud is arctan(2). From point Q (30 m closer), it's arctan(3). How high is the cloud?

example.problem: Solve for the cloud height h.
example.solution: From P: tan(θ₁) = 2, so h / d = 2, giving h = 2d. From Q (30 m closer): tan(θ₂) = 3, so h / (d − 30) = 3. Substituting: 2d / (d − 30) = 3. Solving: 2d = 3d − 90, so d = 90 m. Thus h = 2(90) = 180 m. Verify: from Q, h / (90 − 30) = 180 / 60 = 3. ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine two inverse trig observations to set up a system and solve for unknowns.

slides.title: Using Inverse Trig with Graphs
slides.storyContext: Kavya learns how to read angles from graphs and plots. If you see a point on a unit circle at (0.6, 0.8), you can find the angle using arcsin or arccos.

points.label: Unit circle point (x, y)
points.text: x = cos(θ), y = sin(θ). So θ = arctan(y/x) (with careful attention to quadrant).

points.label: Quadrant adjustment
points.text: arcsin and arctan give angles in limited ranges. For angles in other quadrants, add π or 2π as needed.

example.problem: On a unit circle, a point is at (−0.6, 0.8). Find the angle θ.
example.solution: cos(θ) = −0.6, sin(θ) = 0.8. Since x < 0 and y > 0, angle is in quadrant II. θ = arccos(−0.6) ≈ 2.21 radians ≈ 126.87°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Given coordinates, use inverse trig to find the angle, but check which quadrant you're in.

slides.title: Challenge: Drone Navigation
slides.storyContext: Kavya's drone needs to navigate to a target. It's currently 100 m horizontally from the target and 75 m vertically below. What angle should it fly at to reach the target?

example.problem: Find the angle the drone must fly to reach the target.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the drone's current position and target position to set up a ratio, then apply inverse trig.

slides.title: What Kavya Learned
slides.storyContext: Kavya now reads angles from ratios, a skill that applies to drone navigation, surveying, and architecture.

points.text: Inverse trig functions reverse trig: given a ratio (sine, cosine, tangent), find the angle.
Each inverse has a specific range to ensure it's a true function (bijective on its domain).
arcsin domain [−1,1] → angle [−π/2, π/2]; arccos domain [−1,1] → angle [0, π]; arctan domain ℝ → angle (−π/2, π/2).
Key identity: arcsin(x) + arccos(x) = π/2. Angle of elevation = angle of depression by geometry.
Applications: finding angles of elevation/depression, surveying, architecture, navigation, drone flight paths.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inverse trig functions are your tool when you know ratios and need angles. Essential for real-world geometry and navigation.

subject: Mathematics
title: Rohan's Sports Statistics
hook: Rohan organizes cricket team statistics using matrices, discovering patterns in wins, losses, and runs.

characters.name: Rohan
characters.role: Cricket team captain and stats enthusiast

slides.title: Matrices
slides.storyContext: Rohan's state cricket team needs to organize statistics for 4 matches across 3 categories (runs, wickets, boundaries). Matrices become his organizational tool.

slides.title: The Match Statistics Table
slides.storyContext: Rohan creates a table: Match 1, 2, 3, 4 (columns) × Runs, Wickets, Boundaries (rows). He fills in numbers. Simran says: that's a matrix. Matrices organize data in rows and columns, making calculations easy.

slides.title: What is a Matrix?
slides.storyContext: Simran explains: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns.

points.label: Notation
points.text: A matrix A with m rows and n columns is denoted A_{m×n} or A_{mn}. Element a_{ij} is in row i, column j.

points.label: Square matrix
points.text: If m = n (same number of rows and columns), it's square. Special matrices include identity (main diagonal = 1) and zero (all 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: A matrix is just an organized table of numbers. Rows go horizontal, columns go vertical.

slides.title: Rohan's Data Explosion
slides.storyContext: After 4 matches, Rohan has collected data: Runs [150, 160, 145, 155], Wickets [5, 4, 6, 5], Boundaries [12, 15, 10, 14]. Now he needs to compare matches, add tournaments, analyze trends. Simran says: perfect job for matrix operations.

slides.title: Types of Matrices
slides.storyContext: Rohan and Simran identify special matrix types they'll encounter.

points.label: Row matrix
points.text: Only one row, e.g. [1 2 3] is 1×3.

points.label: Column matrix
points.text: Only one column, e.g. [1; 2; 3] is 3×1.

points.label: Diagonal matrix
points.text: Non-zero elements only on the main diagonal, others zero. Diagonal = {a_{11}, a_{22}, a_{33}, ...}.

points.label: Transpose A^T
points.text: Swap rows and columns. If A is m×n, A^T is n×m. Element (i,j) becomes (j,i).

example.solution: A^T = [[1 4], [2 5], [3 6]]. A is 2×3; A^T is 3×2. Rows become columns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Special matrices include row/column (thin shapes), diagonals (marked elements on the main diagonal), and transposes (flipped rows/columns).

slides.title: Recognizing Matrix Dimensions
slides.storyContext: Rohan practices identifying matrix sizes from examples Simran gives.

points.label: Runs per match [150, 160, 145, 155]
points.text: 1×4 matrix (row matrix: 1 row, 4 columns).

points.label: Player scores in 3 matches [[45, 50, 48], [38, 42, 40], [55, 60, 58]]
points.text: 3×3 matrix (square matrix: 3 rows, 3 columns).

points.label: Transpose of runs: [[150], [160], [145], [155]]
points.text: 4×1 matrix (column matrix: 4 rows, 1 column).

example.problem: If a 2×5 matrix is transposed, what dimensions does the result have?
example.solution: A 5×2 matrix. Transposing swaps rows and columns: 2 rows become 2 columns, 5 columns become 5 rows.

slides.inSimpleWords: Matrix dimension = rows × columns. Transposing swaps them: m×n becomes n×m.

slides.title: Matrix Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Rohan compares two tournaments' statistics (each a 3×4 matrix). He adds matrices element-by-element to get combined stats.

points.label: Addition
points.text: Only matrices of same size can be added. (A + B)_{ij} = A_{ij} + B_{ij}.

points.label: Subtraction
points.text: Likewise: (A − B)_{ij} = A_{ij} − B_{ij}.

points.label: Properties
points.text: Commutative: A + B = B + A. Associative: (A + B) + C = A + (B + C). Additive identity: A + O = A (O is zero matrix).

example.problem: Tournament 1: [[150, 160], [5, 4]]. Tournament 2: [[155, 145], [6, 5]]. Find total stats A + B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add matrices by adding corresponding elements. Like combining two sports scorecards into one summary.

slides.title: Challenge: Adding Tournament Data
slides.storyContext: Rohan has data from 3 tournaments. Tournament A = [[100, 110], [4, 5]], Tournament B = [[120, 115], [5, 4]], Tournament C = [[110, 125], [6, 5]]. Find A + B + C.

example.problem: Add the three matrices.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add multiple matrices in any order (associative); the result is the same.

slides.title: Scalar Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Simran introduces scalar multiplication: multiply every element in a matrix by a constant.

points.label: Definition
points.text: If k is a scalar and A is a matrix, then kA means multiply each element a_{ij} by k.

points.label: Example
points.text: 2 · [[1, 2], [3, 4]] = [[2, 4], [6, 8]]. Every element is doubled.

points.label: Properties
points.text: k(A + B) = kA + kB. Scalar multiplication distributes over addition.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scalar multiplication scales the entire matrix by a constant factor.

slides.title: Matrix Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak asks: if each run is worth 1 point, each wicket is worth 5 points penalty, and each boundary is worth 2 points, what's the total score for each match? Rohan multiplies matrices.

points.label: Rule
points.text: If A is m×n and B is n×p, then AB is m×p. Element (AB)_{ij} = Σ A_{ik} · B_{kj} (sum over k from 1 to n).

points.label: Important
points.text: Only works if columns of A = rows of B. Not commutative: AB ≠ BA usually.

points.label: Scalar multiplication
points.text: Multiply each element by a constant: k·A means multiply each a_{ij} by k.

example.problem: A = [[150, 160, 145]], weights = [[1], [5], [2]]. Find A × weights (score per match).

slides.inSimpleWords: Matrix multiplication combines data and weights. It's like calculating a weighted average, but organized in matrices.

slides.title: Rohan's Weighted Score
slides.storyContext: Coach says: in international cricket, different metrics have different weights. A boundary is more impressive than a dot ball. Rohan creates a weight vector [2, 1, 3] (runs, wickets, boundaries) and multiplies his matrix by it to get a composite score for each match.

slides.title: Step-by-Step Matrix Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Simran walks Rohan through multiplying two matrices step-by-step.
slides.inSimpleWords: For each position in the result, multiply corresponding elements from rows of A and columns of B, then sum.

slides.title: Determinant and Inverse
slides.storyContext: Simran introduces a 2×2 matrix from Rohan's data and explains the determinant (a special number derived from the matrix).

points.label: Determinant of 2×2
points.text: For A = [[a b], [c d]], det(A) = ad − bc.

points.label: Inverse
points.text: If det(A) ≠ 0, A has an inverse: A^{−1} = (1/det(A)) · [[d −b], [−c a]].

points.label: Key property
points.text: A · A^{−1} = I (identity matrix). Inverse only exists if determinant ≠ 0 (matrix is invertible).

slides.inSimpleWords: The determinant is a single number that tells you if a matrix can be inverted. Inverse reverses the matrix's operation.

slides.title: Challenge: Calculating Determinant and Inverse
slides.storyContext: Rohan practices finding inverses. Given A = [[3, 4], [2, 5]], find det(A) and A^{−1}.

example.problem: Find determinant and inverse of [[3, 4], [2, 5]].

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply the determinant formula, then the inverse formula. Always verify A·A^{−1} = I.

slides.title: System of Linear Equations
slides.storyContext: Coach asks: if total runs across 2 matches is 300 and their difference is 10, how many runs in each? Rohan uses matrices to solve.

points.label: Matrix form
points.text: A · X = B, where A is coefficients, X is unknowns, B is constants.

points.label: Solution
points.text: X = A^{−1} · B (if A invertible).

example.problem: Solve x + y = 300; x − y = 10 using matrices.

slides.inSimpleWords: Write a system of equations in matrix form, find the inverse, multiply to solve for unknowns.

slides.title: Rohan Solves a Real Problem
slides.storyContext: Match 1 + Match 2 runs = 300. Match 1 runs − Match 2 runs = 10. Rohan sets up matrices and solves: Match 1 = 155, Match 2 = 145. Coach nods: exactly right. Matrix math works in real life.

slides.title: 3×3 System of Equations (Higher Dimension)
slides.storyContext: Rohan faces a more complex problem: three unknowns, three equations. Matrices still work, though calculating the 3×3 inverse is harder.

points.label: System example
points.text: 2x + y − z = 8; x − y + 2z = 5; 3x + 2y + z = 11. Write as A·X = B.

points.label: A = [[2, 1, −1], [1, −1, 2], [3, 2, 1]]
points.text: The coefficient matrix.

points.label: Solution method
points.text: X = A^{−1}·B (compute 3×3 inverse using cofactor expansion or row reduction).

example.problem: Solve the 3×3 system above using matrices (outline steps, not full calculation).
example.solution: Set up A·X = B. Find det(A). If det(A) ≠ 0, compute A^{−1} using cofactor expansion. Then X = A^{−1}·[[8], [5], [11]]. (Full calculation is lengthy; typically done with calculators or software.)

slides.inSimpleWords: For 3×3 and larger systems, the matrix method still applies, though calculations get tedious without a computer.

slides.title: Challenge: Tournament Scores
slides.storyContext: Rohan has scores from 2 tournaments (each 2×3 matrix: rows = Team A, B; columns = Match 1, 2, 3). He adds them, multiplies by a weights matrix to rank teams.

example.problem: Tournament 1 = [[150 160 145], [140 155 150]]. Tournament 2 = [[160 155 150], [145 160 155]]. Find total, then multiply by [[0.3], [0.3], [0.4]] to get weighted scores.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine matrices by addition, then multiply by weights to prioritize certain matches. Practical data science.

slides.title: Identity and Zero Matrices
slides.storyContext: Simran teaches Rohan about special matrices that behave like 0 and 1 in regular arithmetic.

points.label: Identity matrix I
points.text: All diagonal elements = 1, all others = 0. A · I = A and I · A = A (like multiplying by 1).

points.label: Zero matrix O
points.text: All elements = 0. A + O = A (like adding 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Identity matrix acts like 1 (multiplying by it doesn't change the matrix). Zero matrix acts like 0 (adding it doesn't change things).

slides.title: What Rohan Learned
slides.storyContext: Matrices are Rohan's go-to tool for organizing and analyzing sports data.

points.text: Matrix: rectangular array of m rows and n columns. Element a_{ij} is row i, column j.
Operations: addition (element-wise), subtraction (element-wise), multiplication (combine columns of A with rows of B).
Transpose A^T swaps rows and columns. Matrix multiplication A·B is only defined if columns of A = rows of B.
Determinant = number derived from matrix; only non-zero determinants have inverses.
Inverse A^{−1}: A · A^{−1} = I. Used to solve systems of linear equations: A·X = B → X = A^{−1}·B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Matrices organize numbers. You add, multiply, and invert them like numbers — but element-wise or row-column paired. Powerful for real-world data.
